md: A relative expression has no value until it is anchored. *Present*, *now*, *today*, *last year* and *the past 5 years* all need a reference date, and the normalizer should receive it as an explicit input, never read a hidden clock or let a model guess it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
md: Coverage is an **upper bound** on accuracy. It equals real accuracy only if you have a perfect checker (unit tests, a proof checker). For a math word problem, pass@100 = 83% means 83% of problems have *some* correct sample, not that you can find it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Do not assume more thinking tokens never hurt. Evaluate a reasoning model at several reasoning lengths on your own tasks. Wasted tokens on easy prompts (overthinking) and how to train them away are the subject of the efficient-reasoning course, a follow-on to this one.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
md: Titans' memory update = gradient descent with momentum (carry surprise forward) and weight decay (forget), all gated per token. Momentum keeps writing after a surprising event; forgetting keeps a fixed-size memory from overflowing.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
md: A per-CPU or per-thread cache is a deliberate trade of memory for scalability. Idle rounds look like a leak in heap profiles and in RSS (resident set size, the physical memory a process currently holds), and they multiply by the number of CPUs (or threads) and caches. Every production design pairs its caches with a sizing policy and a way to give memory back.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: From hunt to detection: the FireEye countermeasures
md: Hunts and detections are two ends of one pipeline. Precise, low-volume hunts become alerts; noisy but valuable ones become scheduled hunts with an owner and a review rhythm, like FireEye's supplemental rules. A hunt that never feeds detection leaves the organisation exactly as blind as before, once the hunter moves on.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The Diamond Model: one event, four corners
md: Two traps. First, Type 2 infrastructure is what victims usually see, so an IP address's owner is often another victim, not the adversary. Second, a shared feature is a lead, not a link: two events that share a widely used tool are not necessarily the same adversary (the attribution lesson returns to this).

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
md: Do not let one view take over. The Threat Modeling Manifesto lists *tendency to overfocus* as an anti-pattern: avoid exaggerating attention on adversaries, assets, or techniques. A model built only around a feared attacker misses dull, likely failures.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Compliance is not security. The Senate timeline notes that Target was certified compliant with PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, the card industry's security rules) in September 2013, two months before the breach. An audit checks controls at a moment; a threat model asks how an attacker would get from here to there.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A random train/test split on a time series leaks the future into training and makes every model look better than it will be in production. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos state the rule plainly: the training set may contain only observations that occurred before the test observations, so no future observations are used to construct the forecast.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
md: Downgrade defence has two halves: **authenticate the negotiation** (transcript signatures, the sentinel, SCSV) and **delete the weak options** so there is nothing to downgrade to. The second is the one that always works.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: A Triton program instance is not one thread. It is closer to a CUDA thread block: one program becomes `num_warps` warps of 32 threads each, so with the default `num_warps=4` a single program runs on 128 threads.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
md: The rule that keeps any mask honest: a position may only attend to what will exist when it is generated. Bidirectional attention inside an image is legal exactly when the whole image is produced together, as in diffusion, flow or masked prediction. Under token-by-token generation it would leak the answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Running an unmodified binary on a unikernel does not get you function-call costs. Trapping and translating each `syscall` cost 84 cycles in Unikraft's measurement, 21 times a function call. Relinking against the libOS is what removes the crossing.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes
md: Unikernel gains split into **removing the crossing** (small for real applications, per Lupine) and **specializing** (large). Linux can deliver much of the second. Choose a libOS unikernel when you also want tiny images, millisecond boots and a minimal attack surface, and can accept its limits.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Batching queries: from memory-bound scans to matrix multiply
md: Batching Q queries raises intensity from 0.5 to Q/2 FLOP per byte by reusing each fetched vector. It turns a flat scan into a GEMM plus a top-k selection, and the selection becomes the next bottleneck. It does nothing for a single query, and graph walks cannot share fetches this way.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: When a write becomes searchable: refresh, replicas and consistency
md: Acknowledged, durable and visible are three different moments, and on a replicated shard each replica reaches them at its own time. Every engine lets you pay latency to close the gap: wait=true or refresh=wait_for for your own writes, more acknowledging replicas for writes, majority or Strong reads for everyone.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: The V1 trainer: TransferQueue, sync and async modes, partial rollout
md: Async is not free. Every async mode trains on tokens from older weights, so pair it with a staleness bound and a correction mode, and watch `training/off_policy/*`. `separate_async` also needs a network checkpoint engine (`nccl`, `nixl` or `mooncake`, not `naive`) and its batch invariant, or startup fails.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
md: FVD alone cannot tell whether a model listens to actions. A model that ignores the controls but produces realistic clips can score well. That is why Genie pairs FVD with delta PSNR, and why its pixel-input LAM was chosen despite a slightly worse Platformers FVD (40.1 vs 38.8): its controllability was much higher (1.91 vs 1.33).

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Case: VENOM, the floppy controller every guest had
md: VENOM's lasting lesson is about inventory, not floppies: a legacy device that "cannot be removed or disabled" was guest-reachable on every x86 VM. Know which device models your VMs expose, prefer machine types with fewer of them, and sandbox the process that runs them.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
md: Library checkpoints may differ slightly from this count. Hugging Face's `ViTModel` can include an extra pooler layer (a D x D dense plus tanh); `ViTForImageClassification` builds the backbone without it and reads the raw CLS state. Always check with a parameter count on the actual model rather than trusting a model card.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Why per-step tokens break at 50 Hz, and how FAST compresses them
md: FAST spends tokens on information, not on time steps. Across datasets from 5 Hz to 50 Hz it produced roughly 30 tokens per arm per 1-second chunk, so the token count tracks the complexity of the motion rather than the control rate.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
md: TiTok's 32 tokens are not an image patch each. Flattening a 2D grid into a sequence still keeps the grid constraint; a 1D tokenizer lets each token describe any part of the image. Ids from different tokenizers are not interchangeable even at the same length.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: FP8 KV caches inside the backends: scales, kernels, support
md: An FP8 cache can silently move you to another backend. On an A100 (FA2), FLASH_ATTN fails validation for any FP8 cache and selection falls to FLASHINFER. On an H100, `fp8_e5m2` does the same. If you also pinned `--attention-backend FLASH_ATTN`, startup fails instead. Check the selector's log line after changing the cache dtype.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
md: Tiling only helps up to the largest grid the model was trained with. Beyond that the image is downscaled again, and text that was 10 px tall becomes 5 px tall. Check the preprocessing config of the model you deploy, not just the paper.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
md: Compare&swap is **universal**: an object with consensus number at least $n$ can implement any object wait-free for $n$ processes (next lesson). Fetch&add, swap and test&set are not, so Herlihy proves you cannot build a wait-free compare&swap out of them plus registers for three or more processes.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Rolling a 6-hour step out to 10 days
md: Blurry long-range output from an MSE-trained model is not a bug in the network. It is exactly what MSE asks for under uncertainty. Lesson 5 shows how ensembles and CRPS avoid it.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Recon at bounty scale: wildcards, subdomains and live hosts
md: Recon results are candidates, not permission. A name found in a CT log, a JavaScript file or a scanner's output is tested only if the policy's scope covers it, and never if the policy excludes it.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Reading a programme policy: scope, rules and safe harbour
md: Scope, rules and safe harbour are read together: an in-scope asset tested with a banned method, or with someone else's account, is outside the protection. Safe harbour never extends to third parties the programme does not control.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookie attributes: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, prefixes
md: HttpOnly is often oversold. It stops cookie **theft** by script, so an attacker cannot carry the session to their own machine. It does not stop script running in your page from **using** the session right there, which is what the Samy worm did. XSS still needs to be prevented at its source.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: PowerShell: objects in a pipeline, and why attackers like it
md: Misconception: "execution policy stops malicious PowerShell". It does not. Treat it as a seat belt for honest users, and rely on logging, AMSI and application control for security.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WEP: how a 24-bit IV broke Wi-Fi's first encryption
md: A longer WEP key does not help. SP 800-97: the technique "has known flaws that are not mitigated by longer keys". The problems are the tiny IV, the linear checksum and RC4's key schedule, none of which depend on key length. If a device only supports WEP, treat its traffic as unencrypted and isolate it.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Android: UID sandbox, SELinux, verified boot and Play Protect
md: Rooting a phone (gaining root, Unix's all-powerful user) or unlocking its bootloader deliberately removes layers described here: verified boot no longer vouches for the system, and root can override the UID sandbox. Fine for a lab device, a serious risk on one that holds work data; device management and attestation checks such as the Play Integrity API (lesson 16) let organisations detect it.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot
md: Tokio's local queue is FIFO, not LIFO: the owner pops from the same end thieves steal from. For servers made of many independent tasks, fairness (no task waits forever behind newer ones) matters more than depth-first order. Locality comes from the LIFO slot instead, which Tokio uses at most 3 times in a row to prevent two tasks from starving the queue by waking each other.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy means removing the **CPU copies between the page cache, user memory and socket buffers**. Device DMA still happens. The win scales with bytes moved, so it matters when a program mostly shovels data it does not inspect.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Classifying with labels chosen at inference time
md: In a zero-shot classifier, the label text plays the role of the trained weights. Changing a label's wording changes the classifier, so wording, templates, and descriptions are design decisions you test, not decoration.
